title: Luxury stocks: how to analyze luxury companies
description: Luxury stocks live on the brand: 66% gross margin against the median's 48%. Pricing power, the pyramid and the cycle — with LVMH worked through.
author: AK1A Research Lab
body:
Luxury stocks are shares in companies that sell status goods — bags, watches, perfume, champagne — where much of the price tag is a story the consumer pays for, not a cost of goods. The sector is analytically its own world for three reasons. First, profitability lives not in volume but in pricing power: LVMH, the world's largest luxury group with more than 75 houses, keeps 66.4 percent of every revenue euro after the cost of goods — against the consumer branch's median of 48.3 percent in AK1A's analysis universe. Second, demand is not cycle-neutral: luxury consumption swings with markets, currencies and sentiment — cyclical, though the goods are sold as timeless. Third, the brand is the asset itself — but internally built, in practice booked at zero.

This guide walks the mechanics: pricing power and its limit, the pyramid behind the 2025 divide, the post-boom cycle and five points of report reading — LVMH worked through on universe data (public market sources, retrieved 2026-09-03) and the official annual report for 2025. The consumer companies guide and the food track are the neighbors: there the store and the shelf product stand at the center — here the status good.

## Luxury stocks and pricing power — the mechanics

For an ordinary good the law of demand holds: higher price, lower volume. For the status good it can invert — the price is part of the product, and a bag costing three times more is not the same bag but a more exclusive one. Economics names it the Veblen good, after Thorstein Veblen — the business model in a sentence: value is created in the story, not the factory.

Put numbers on it: of a hundred euros paid for a product from LVMH's portfolio — Louis Vuitton, Dior, Tiffany, Sephora — 66.4 remain after the cost of goods. Among the universe's sixteen consumer companies the median is 48.3 percent; among goods manufacturers only the gaming company Evolution stands higher (100 percent — software without cost of goods in the classical sense), with Coca-Cola's concentrate model at 61.9. The difference from an ordinary manufacturer is not factory efficiency but who carries the pricing power — brand strength measured in [Brand & customer loyalty](/kurser/v14-varumarke), the margin as a measure in [Gross margin](/kurser/v07-bruttomarginal).

The power has a limit, visible in volume. Pricing power is price increases without volume loss: raise prices 6 percent with volume held and organic growth becomes 6.0 percent (1.06 × 1.00); lose 8 percent of volume and it becomes minus 2.5 percent (1.06 × 0.92 = 0.975). The same price increase, two realities — the difference lives in brand durability. The arithmetic is trained in [Revenue growth](/kurser/v01-forsaljningstillvaxt).

## The pyramid — the aspiration consumer disappears first

The luxury market is often described as a pyramid. At the top stand houses where demand exceeds supply: volume deliberately held short, waiting lists normal, price increases passing without volume loss. Hermès is the archetype, full-year 2025 the proof — record revenue 16 billion euro, growth 9 percent at constant rates (5.5 percent reported), operating margin 30.3 percent. In the middle and bottom stands the aspiration consumer: the one buying the entry product — perfume, sunglasses, the smaller bag — while the margin lasts, striking it first when it does not.

LVMH spans the whole pyramid, from Louis Vuitton and Dior at the top to Sephora and perfumes at the bottom, with watches and champagne between. The breadth is a strength in the upturn — every step has a house — and an exposure in the downturn: the middle's and bottom's consumers disappear first. 2025 showed the divide in black and white: same sector, two outcomes. Hermès grew 9 percent at constant rates; LVMH fell 4.6 percent in reported revenue. The difference is not primarily management but where in the pyramid the brand stands — place every company in the pyramid before reading the multiple.

## The cycle — from boom to normalization, worked through

LVMH's series in the universe, billion euro: revenue 79.2 (2022), 86.2 (2023), 84.7 (2024) and 80.8 (2025) — two falling years, minus 1.7 and minus 4.6 percent. The profit series: 15.2, 12.6 and 10.9; the 2025 net profit fell 13.3 percent, and the source's growth rate across the four fiscal years lands at minus 8.2 percent per year. Read without context, a structural loser; read with the base year in mind, a normalization from an exceptional boom — pandemic pent-up consumption broke loose in 2021–2023, lifting both volume and price. The base year decides the picture.

The official 2025 annual report adds nuance: operating profit 17.8 billion euro, operating margin 22 percent — in line with the universe's EBIT margin of 22.5. The bottom of the income statement weighs in tax, minorities and items affecting comparability; the operating side shows the business. Reading the double track is trained in [Notes — the hidden information](/kurser/km-004-noter).

The multiple weighs between the pictures: P/E 19.7 trailing, but consensus expects plus 12.3 percent in earnings per share next year — forward P/E 19.7 ÷ 1.123 ≈ 17.6. EV/EBIT stands at 13.5, the free cash flow yield at 5.5 percent. PEG 1.59 — with the caveat that the base year sits in the post-boom, the forecast year in the normalization; the ratio then says more about cycle than valuation ([the weaknesses of the PEG multiple](/blogg/peg-multipeln-svagheter-2026), [the P/E deep dive](/kurser/km-009-pe)). And like all stable cash flows, luxury multiples are rate-sensitive — rising rates cut the value of distant cash flows without the business changing.

## Returns, the balance sheet and control

Profitability: ROE 16.6 percent and ROIC 17.0 percent — nearly even. A different structure from the food duopoly, where leverage carried part of the high ROE: here the return lives in the business and the balance sheet is calm, with 0.53 of debt per unit of equity. When ROE and ROIC hold together, profit is created in the brand, not the financing — the mechanics in [ROE](/kurser/v09-roe), the measure critique in [ROIC — the forgotten key ratio](/blogg/roic-den-glomda-nyckeltalen-v11).

Control is the sector's special chapter. The Arnault family owns, through the holding Agache, 50.01 percent of capital and 65.94 percent of votes (February 2026) — double voting rights for long-term ownership under French company law, the same principle as Swedish A and B shares. The consequence is worth remembering: board composition and succession are decided within the family, not on the exchange — no share price can vote control home.

## Reading the report — five points

- **Organic growth, split into price and volume.** LVMH reports comparable growth with currencies and acquisitions stripped; price increases with volume held are the brand holding.
- **The direction of the gross margin.** The level shows the brand position, the movement the tug-of-war between pricing and costs.
- **The business groups.** Fashion & Leather Goods carries the profitability; watches, jewelry and spirits swing heavier — read per segment before the whole, as in [the quarterly report](/kurser/km-006-kvartalsrapporten).
- **The geography.** The Chinese consumer's cycle — stocks, property, sentiment — is the sector's largest single swing factor; read the region lines.
- **The currency.** Report in euro, sales in dollars, yuan and yen. Hermès 2025 is the textbook case: 9 percent at constant rates became 5.5 percent reported.

## The summary

- Pricing power is the business model: gross margin 66.4 percent against the consumer median's 48.3 — the story, not the factory, carries the margin.
- The pyramid decides the cycle round: Hermès at the top grew 9 percent at constant rates in 2025; LVMH across the whole pyramid fell 4.6 — the aspiration consumer disappears first.
- The cycle: 86.2 → 80.8 billion euro 2023–2025, net profit minus 13.3 percent in 2025, CAGR minus 8.2 percent per year from a boom base year — the base year decides the picture.
- The multiple: trailing 19.7 against forward 17.6 on consensus plus 12.3 percent; EV/EBIT 13.5 and PEG 1.59 with a cycle caveat.
- Returns without leverage drama: ROE 16.6 and ROIC 17.0 percent, debt to equity 0.53.
- Control: the Arnault family, 50.01 percent capital and 65.94 percent votes — governance is not decided on the exchange.

The continuation track: [the luxury sector](/kurser/se-05-lyxsektorn) deepens every theme here, [the sector medians](/blogg/branschmedianer-akm2) show where the consumer branch stands, and [the complete guide to Swedish stock analysis](/blogg/komplett-guide-svensk-aktieanalys-2026) places the method in the whole.
